extracted.intended_audience: psychologists, experimentalists, and educated readers interested in mental imagery and psychological measurement
extracted.subtask_description: Designing, administering, and scoring a questionnaire-based inquiry into individual differences in visual mental imagery (brightness, definition, colour, vividness, completeness, and related faculties). Includes sampling and classification guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Illumination
rubrics_metrics.description: Is the image dim or fairly clear? Is its brightness comparable to that of the actual scene?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as an explicit questionnaire item. Responses range from 'Brilliant, distinct, never blotchy' to 'Dim and not comparable in brightness to the real scene.' Examples from returns: 'Brightness as in the actual scene.'; 'Bright, comparable to real scene.'; 'Dim and indistinct.' This dimension is incorporated into the later statistical classification (octiles, quartiles, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition
rubrics_metrics.description: Are all the objects pretty well defined at the same time, or is the place of sharpest definition at any one moment more contracted than in a real scene?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Question explicitly asks about how sharply-defined objects are in the mental image. Example response categories: 'All clear and bright; all the objects seem to me well defined at the same time.'; 'Fairly clear, but not equal to the scene. Defined, but not sharply; not all seen with equal clearness.'; 'Badly defined with blotches of light.' Use in scoring to distinguish those who can visualise whole scenes versus only individual salient items.

rubrics_metrics.name: Colouring / Colour representation
rubrics_metrics.description: Are the colours of objects in the image distinct and natural? (e.g., colours of china, toast, parsley, etc.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicit questionnaire item. Sample graded returns: 'Perfectly distinct, bright, and natural.'; 'All details seen perfectly.'; 'Fairly distinct, though not certain that they are accurately recalled.'; 'Faint; can only recall colours by a special effort.' Many respondents report either vivid natural colouring or nil power. This metric is reported separately (see 'COLOUR REPRESENTATION') and used in the octile/quartile classification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vividness of mental imagery (overall)
rubrics_metrics.description: Overall strength/vividness of the mental image (composite judgment of clarity, brightness, definition, completeness).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author classifies returns into ordered ranks (e.g., 'Cases where the faculty is very high', 'mediocre', 'lowest') with illustrative verbatim responses. Examples for 'very high': 'Brilliant, distinct, never blotchy.'; 'Quite comparable to the real object.' For 'mediocre': 'Fairly clear; details rather misty.' For 'lowest': 'No power of visualising.' The text recommends judging the faculty from the whole of replies and other knowledge of the writer, then using statistical treatment (octiles, quartiles). Note cautionary points: some respondents (including artists) may overestimate ability to draw from their mental images.

rubrics_metrics.name: Completeness vs. partial/fragmentary imagery
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the respondent can visualise the whole scene at once or only single objects/parts in succession.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'I can recall any single object or group of objects, but not the whole table at once.'; 'I can pass my eyes down the table and see the different things distinctly, but not the whole table at once.'; 'I can recall the breakfast-table but do not see it.' Use this to distinguish those whose images require sequential attention versus simultaneous comprehension; relevant for scoring (e.g., 'First Quartile' vs 'Last Quartile').

rubrics_metrics.name: Ability to draw/produce from imagery
rubrics_metrics.description: Claimed capacity to draw accurately from one's mental image (whether the person could reproduce the image on paper).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many respondents assert 'If I could draw, I am sure I could draw perfectly from my mental image.' But the author warns of unconscious exaggeration: artists sometimes discover gaps when attempting to draw. Use empirical tests (attempted drawing) rather than self-report alone when possible; consider this an anti-pattern of overconfident self-assessment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comprehension of multiple perspectives / simultaneous aspects
rubrics_metrics.description: Ability to imagine more than can be seen at one moment by the eyes, e.g., all sides of a solid, stereoscopic or panoramic combination, or 'touch-sight' encompassing many aspects together.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reported phenomena include imagining all sides of a crystal at once, stereoscopic rounding, or embracing an entire sphere in a single perception. Use as a distinct metric: some can 'visualise at the same moment all round the image of a solid body' while others cannot. Includes examples like chess blindfold play and mental sliding-rule use as functional demonstrations of complex visualisation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Independence from other faculties (vision, dreaming, recognition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Consideration that visualising power may be independent of sharp sight, dreaming frequency, or face-recognition ability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text emphasises that 'sharp sight is [not] accompanied by clear visual memory' and that visualising 'does not go with dreaming' necessarily, nor always with quick recognition. Use this as interpretive guidance: do not infer one faculty from another; evaluate imagery on its own dimensions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Question framing and openness (survey design)
rubrics_metrics.description: Frame questions to avoid misunderstanding, admit easy reply, cover the ground, and tempt correspondents to write freely in fuller explanation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author notes 'There is hardly any more difficult task than that of framing questions which are not likely to be misunderstood... I did my best... to tempt my correspondents to write freely in fuller explanation of their replies.' Practical guidance: include clear instructions (example prompt: 'think of some definite object... consider carefully the picture that rises before your mind's eye'), combine set questions with invitations for free description, and cross-question respondents to increase trustworthiness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sampling and respondent-selection considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Be aware of non-haphazard samples, response biases, and group differences (e.g., scientific men vs. general society, schoolboys).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author recognises limitations: returns from friends and correspondents are not strictly haphazard; many who lack the faculty or who cannot express it sent no returns. He compares groups (scientific men, general society, school returns) and uses cross-examination and teacher-mediated explanations to increase data quality. Use multiple sources and note probable selection effects when interpreting frequencies (e.g., 'scientific men... protested that mental imagery was unknown to them').

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification and statistical scoring procedure
rubrics_metrics.description: Method of classifying replies into ordered ranks and using statistical groupings (octiles, quartiles, suboctiles, 'middlemost', highest/lowest) for summary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author 'classified according to the order of the faculty, as judged to the best of my ability from the whole of what was said...' and then reports grouped summaries (Highest; First Suboctile; First Octile; First Quartile; Middlemost; Last Quartile; Last Octile; Last Suboctile; Lowest). He refers to a chapter of statistics for the treatment. Guidance: use whole-text judgment per respondent, then place respondents into quantile-based bins to summarise distributional properties of the faculty.
